items.title: Biodigital Transformation and Multidisciplinary Treatment Planning in Dentistry
items.abstract: Digitalization in dentistry signifies a new era that goes beyond transferring imaging, impression-taking, design, and manufacturing stages to computer-aided systems and requires biological characteristics, clinical findings, patient preferences, and long-term risks to be evaluated within a shared data model. In this chapter, “biodigital dentistry” is defined as the integration of patients’ clinical, radiological, morphological, functional, and, when necessary, molecular data through digital technologies and the use of this integrated information in diagnosis, treatment simulation, interdisciplinary sequencing, manufacturing, and monitoring processes. The historical development of the transition from conventional to digital workflows, virtual patient creation, clinical–radiological–digital data fusion, artificial intelligence-assisted decision-support systems, the timing of periodontal–orthodontic–surgical–restorative treatments, and personalized care models are discussed in light of current evidence. Ethical and legal issues, including algorithmic bias, explainability, data minimization, cybersecurity, informed consent, and the domestic and international transfer of health data, are also evaluated in terms of clinical applicability. The principal objective of the biodigital transformation is not to replace the clinician but to facilitate more predictable decision-making for the right patient, at the right time, and within biological limits. Successful implementation requires an interoperable data infrastructure, validated technologies, shared interdisciplinary objectives, human oversight, and continuous outcome monitoring.

items.title: Biological Variability and Biomedical Innovation in Personalized Orthodontics: A Systematic Review with Narrative Synthesis
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Orthodontic treatment response varies considerably among patients because mechanical loading interacts with individual biological, anatomical, systemic, and behavioral characteristics. Advances in mechanobiology, molecular biomarkers, omics technologies, and artificial intelligence (AI) may support a more personalized approach to treatment. This systematic review (SR) aimed to evaluate human clinical evidence concerning these domains and their potential contribution to predicting orthodontic response, improving clinical decision-making, and reducing adverse effects. Methods: A systematic search of PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science was conducted through June 2026. Primary studies involving human participants and addressing orthodontic tooth movement (OTM), biological variability, biomarkers, genomics, epigenetics, multi-omics, or AI-supported orthodontics were selected according to predefined eligibility criteria. The review was conducted and reported in accordance with Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020, and heterogeneous evidence was synthesized narratively across four predefined domains. The review protocol was registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO; registration number CRD420261486348). Risk of bias was assessed using design-appropriate instruments. Certainty of evidence was assessed at the outcome level using GRADE principles adapted to narrative synthesis. Results: The search identified 1051 records, of which 14 primary human studies were included. The clinical evidence comprised randomized trials, longitudinal and cross-sectional biomarker studies, genetic association studies, and a case report. Molecular and multi-omics studies identified candidate markers of biological response and patient phenotype. The included computational studies examined genetic association rules, gingival-enlargement classification, and AI-assisted root-resorption measurement; none demonstrated AI-guided selection of orthodontic forces. However, small samples, methodological heterogeneity, limited adjustment for confounding, and lack of external validation restricted clinical translation. Certainty of evidence supporting clinical personalization applications was predominantly very low. Conclusions: Personalized orthodontics should remain grounded in comprehensive diagnosis, biologically compatible mechanics, and individualized monitoring. Molecular and computational tools may complement clinical assessment, but routine implementation requires standardized protocols, multicenter validation, and prospective evidence of patient-relevant benefit.

items.title: Blockchain Security: An Empirical Evaluation of High‐Impact Exploits and Detection Tools
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Blockchain introduced secure, peer‐to‐peer transactions in decentralized environments without reliance on central authorities. However, attackers continue to exploit blockchain projects. Over the past decade, reported blockchain exploit losses have exceeded $24 billion. Although existing research analyzes blockchain vulnerabilities and real‐world incidents, many studies focus on specific vulnerability classes or smart contract issues only. Therefore, we present an empirical study of major blockchain exploits from 2020 to 2025. Based on detailed analysis of these exploits, we introduce a practitioner‐oriented taxonomy that organizes the dominant root causes observed in the analyzed exploits across four domains: Human Risks, Off‐Chain Infrastructure Vulnerabilities, Private Key Compromises, and Smart Contract Vulnerabilities. Across these categories, we present case studies, code illustrations where applicable, and mitigation strategies. Moreover, we evaluate five vulnerability‐detection tools spanning four paradigms, namely static analysis ( Slither , 4naly3er ), symbolic execution ( Mythril ), bounded/formal verification ( SMTChecker ), and LLM‐assisted analysis ( GPTScan ), on a curated test suite of vulnerable and secure contracts. Our results show detection gaps under the evaluated setting: Slither, Mythril, and 4naly3er all scored recall below 40%. SMTChecker and GPTScan were evaluated separately because of their narrower target scopes. SMTChecker detected only arithmetic issues, while GPTScan produced no benchmark‐relevant detections. The study highlights the high average loss associated with smart contract access‐control failures, the need for post‐deployment monitoring beyond one‐time audits, and risks related to Off‐Chain Infrastructure Vulnerabilities. By analyzing exploits and offering mitigations, we provide a structured reference for identifying, prioritizing, and mitigating major blockchain security risks.

items.title: Bridging Epistemologies: Integrating Faith into STEM Education and Its Impact on Student Learning Outcomes
items.abstract: Background: Global STEM reforms increasingly privilege technical proficiency while sidelining moral teleology, leaving graduates adept with code but adrift on questions of purpose. This study advances a Scripture‑anchored, interdisciplinary framework that reunites scientific inquiry with a Christian worldview and empirically tests its influence on student learning. Methodology: Adopting a qualitative‑dominant mixed‑methods design, we executed an AI‑assisted meta‑synthesis of 180 peer‑reviewed sources (2019‑2025) and triangulated those insights with multi‑site case studies of Wheaton College (USA), Daystar University (Kenya), and Redeemer University (Canada). Data—curricula, alumni surveys, and classroom artefacts—underwent thematic coding and cross‑case pattern matching, generating testable propositions linking faith‑based instruction, epistemic coherence, and learning outcomes. Results: Across contexts, faith‑integrated STEM programmes exhibited markedly greater cognitive engagement, deeper ethical reasoning, and heightened spiritual formation than secular comparators. Meta‑synthesised effect sizes (Hedges g = 0.35–0.55) show that explicit biblical framing elevates moral‑reasoning and purpose metrics, with the most pronounced gains among students previously unfamiliar with faith‑learning integration. Key mediators include faculty integration skill, mission‑aligned accreditation standards, and culturally attuned pedagogy. Conclusions: Positioning sola Scriptura as the ultimate epistemic authority does not dilute scientific rigour; it re‑humanises STEM by welding empirical facts to transcendent purpose. The proposed framework supplies educators, policymakers, and accreditation bodies with a scalable roadmap for producing technically competent, ethically resilient graduates equipped to steward AI, biotechnology, and green‑tech frontiers. Future research should deploy longitudinal, multi‑institutional designs and neurocognitive measures to further validate the model’s causal pathways and global applicability.

items.title: Bridging the AI use–competence gap
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming graduate research and academic work; however, increased use does not necessarily lead to critical evaluation or responsible engagement. This study examines the gap between graduate students’ AI use and their evaluative, ethical, and rhetorical engagement with AI-generated outputs. Using a survey-based exploratory case study design, the study draws on data from 50 graduate students across four national contexts, complemented by open-ended responses and contextual observations. Findings reveal high levels of AI use alongside limited verification practices, ethical uncertainty, and a tendency to view AI outputs as neutral or authoritative, indicating a persistent use–competence gap. The study proposes a holistic AI literacy framework with implications for curriculum, assessment, and policy.

items.title: CAD/CAM Technologies, Three-Dimensional Printing, and Contemporary Dental Materials
items.abstract: CAD/CAM technologies have transformed the production of fixed prosthodontic restorations from a craft based on manual skill into a standardized and measurable digital process. This chapter addresses, for dental students in their clinical years and for early-career clinicians, the fundamental principles of CAD/CAM systems, digital and artificial intelligence-assisted restoration design, milling and three-dimensional printing technologies, contemporary restorative materials, the factors influencing material selection, accuracy and quality control in digital manufacturing, and the biocompatible and smart materials of the future, in the light of the current and verified literature. The digital workflow comprises three interdependent links—data acquisition, design, and manufacturing—and the quality of the final restoration is limited by the weakest link in the chain. Although milling remains the gold standard for definitive restorations, additive manufacturing has become established for interim restorations, models, and surgical guides, and it is a rapidly maturing alternative for definitive restorations. On the material side, the rise of monolithic zirconia, the diversification of lithium silicate glass-ceramics, and the establishment of resin-matrix ceramics in minimally invasive applications offer the clinician a broad range of options with varying levels of evidence. Current systematic-review and meta-analytic evidence shows that AI-assisted design shortens design time and improves reproducibility, but that human oversight remains indispensable. Clinical success depends on manufacturing the right material with validated parameters for the right indication and applying it with an appropriate adhesive or conventional cementation protocol. Accuracy should be defined by its trueness and precision components, marginal fit should be evaluated against clinical acceptability thresholds, and quality control should be maintained at every link of the digital chain. The graded, bioactive, self-healing, and stimuli-responsive materials of the future, together with additively manufactured ceramics, signal a transition from passive to smart materials in restorative dentistry.

items.title: Can artificial intelligence produce lawyers or merely law graduates? The crisis of competency in South African legal education
items.abstract: The rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into higher education is fundamentally reshaping how students access and present knowledge. Within legal education particularly, AI tools increasingly enable students to generate summaries, conduct research, draft legal content and retrieve information with minimal engagement in traditional legal reasoning processes. At the same time, South African law faculties remain tasked with cultivating industry ready candidate legal practitioners who possess critical thinking abilities, ethical judgment, persuasive communication skills as well as strong legal research competencies. This creates an important pedagogical tension. While AI may enhance efficiency and technological fluency, its uncritical use may simultaneously undermine the intellectual rigour required for competent legal practice. This paper critically examines whether the growing integration of AI in legal education supports or compromises the cultivation of graduate attributes required within the South African legal profession. Using a doctrinal and conceptual methodology, the study analyses the graduate competency frameworks advanced by the Council on Higher Education and the South African Qualifications Authority. It further interrogates whether AI tools meaningfully contribute toward the development of legal reasoning, ethical sensitivity, drafting proficiency and contextual interpretation, all of which remain central to professional legal readiness. The paper argues that although AI presents significant opportunities for enhancing legal research efficiency and technological competence, overreliance on these tools risks producing graduates who are technologically capable yet jurisprudentially underdeveloped. It contends that AI cannot replace the human processes of critical engagement, ethical reflection and contextual legal interpretation that define legal education within a constitutional democracy. The study concludes that responsible AI integration in legal education requires careful pedagogical design and ethical oversight to ensure that innovation does not come at the expense of professional competence and intellectual integrity.

items.title: Can Language Models Play the Wikipedia Game?
items.abstract: Language models increasingly support or automate information retrieval from document collections too large to index. This task is difficult when it requires specialist linguistic or scientific knowledge. We used the Wikipedia Game to test language models on an analogous information retrieval task. In the game, players must reach a target article using only article links. We compared sentence embedding models and LLMs across five Wikipedia languages and five academic-literature datasets. We construct very large local graphs of Wikipedia pages and of paper citations using OpenAlex and provide code to build and navigate them. This allows the study of language models' navigation capabilities without relying on third-party APIs. We compared the models with human and TF-IDF benchmarks. The Wikipedia Game format enables robust comparisons across techniques, languages, and domains. No model significantly outperformed humans, although the best models (GPT-o3 mini, GPT-4o, QwQ:32B, and DeepSeek-R1:70B) achieved comparable success. Performance and rankings varied across languages and topics, with implications for practitioners utilising these techniques.

items.title: Can machines reason non-verbally?
items.abstract: Modern machines can solve equations, follow logic and reason through language, yet they still struggle with problems that require visual non-verbal reasoning. This is evident even in advanced systems such as DeepSeek, ChatGPT and Gemini, which remain limited on visual tasks such as completing abstract patterns or delineating ambiguous regions-of-interest. Unlike explicit intermediate steps in verbal reasoning which can be verified through logic or automated tests, visual reasoning involves implicit intermediate steps with no clear methods for verification. Non-verbal reasoning is therefore challenging to model and, as a result, remains a fundamental limitation of current machine intelligence. Here we introduce GenVerOpt, a general framework that unifies generation, verification and optimisation into a reasoning pipeline for machines. By generating candidate solutions, verifying their correctness, and iteratively refining them, GenVerOpt enables per-sample optimisation rather than relying solely on dataset-level trends captured during model training. This process mirrors human problem-solving where multiple possibilities are imagined, evaluated, and refined until a correct solution emerges. Across diverse domains, GenVerOpt demonstrates capabilities beyond existing systems: it surpasses humans on abstract IQ puzzles, matches clinicians in prostate cancer segmentation, exceeds experts in liver vessel reconstruction and outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in tumour boundary alignment. These results show that machine reasoning can extend beyond language, establishing visual non-verbal reasoning as a foundation for more flexible and generalisable intelligence.

items.title: CB-Orchestrator: Adaptive Workflow Optimization for LLM Agents via Contextual Bandits
items.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in tackling complex tasks through agentic workflows. However, manually designing these workflows is labor-intensive and lacks flexibility to adapt to diverse queries. While automated workflow optimization is a promising direction, existing methods often incur expensive API costs during training-phase feedback collection. Furthermore, they fail to adaptively reuse high-quality workflows, which creates a bottleneck for both performance and cost-effectiveness. To address these limitations, we propose CB-Orchestrator, an adaptive framework that decouples workflow generation from selection. In the first stage, we construct a diverse pool of candidate workflows via evolutionary search. In the second stage, we formulate workflow selection as a Contextual Bandit problem, which enables sample-efficient learning by balancing exploration and exploitation, thereby significantly reducing the feedback required for training. During inference, the model adaptively selects the optimal workflow tailored to each query. Evaluations across five diverse benchmarks demonstrate that CB-Orchestrator consistently outperforms all baselines. Notably, on the MATH dataset, CB-Orchestrator achieves better performance than strong recent baselines while reducing training-phase API token overhead by no less than 40.55% and total end-to-end training (including workflow pool generation) token overhead by no less than 29.73%.

items.abstract: In recent years, access to online health information has undergone a radical and profound transformation: we have moved from the passive information model of search engines (“Dr. Google”) to active, conversational interaction with chatbots based on large language models (LLMs). This shift represents not only a technological evolution but also an anthropological change in how patients interpret their own experience of illness and build their relationship with their doctor. A qualitative comparative analysis was conducted on five chatbots (GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Grok 4 Veloce, and DeepSeek), presenting each with the same seven medical questions in separate chats on the same day, using free-access versions to simulate the average user’s experience. Findings highlight the risk of a progressive disintermediation of medical knowledge, accompanied by phenomena of conversational manipulation and an implicit redefinition of clinical authority. In this context, the patient arrives at the consultation no longer as a seeker of information, but as an already informed interlocutor, carrying expectations, beliefs, and very often a self-diagnosis. This dynamic gives rise to an ethical disorientation involving both parties: patients, who may be influenced by simulated relational interractions, and physicians, who face a perceived erosion of epistemic authority. In light of this, there is a need to rethink and reframe the therapeutic relationship as an encounter between human vulnerabilities, in which artificial intelligence may serve as a supportive tool, but cannot replace the relational, ethical, and responsible dimension of medical practice

items.title: Chem-AI: Reframing AI-Assisted Research Through Structured, Retrieval-Based Scientific Literature Analysis
items.abstract: The growing volume of scientific literature presents a significant challenge for researchers to identify relevant methods, compare findings, and build upon existing work. Although advances in artificial intelligence have led to new tools for literature analysis, many of these tools rely on generative models whose outputs are not always grounded in verifiable sources. This raises concerns about reliability and reproducibility in scientific research. In this study, we explore whether a retrieval-based system can provide more transparent and trustworthy support throughout the research process. We present Chem-AI, an interactive tool that structures the research process into clear steps, including query interpretation, literature retrieval, experiment classification, and method mapping. Unlike conventional AI systems that generate answers without clear justification, Chem-AI links each output directly to published research, allowing users to trace and verify the information. The system was evaluated using a diverse set of chemistry research queries spanning reaction mechanisms and analytical techniques. Compared to standard generative models, Chem-AI retrieved more relevant sources (with roughly 95% of responses rated as fully relevant), produced responses grounded in established methods, and reduced unsupported or unverifiable claims. These results suggest that a retrieval-based approach improves both the reliability and clarity of AI-assisted research. By aligning with the structure of real research workflows, Chem-AI provides a more transparent and user-centered way to navigate scientific literature. This approach is especially useful for undergraduate researchers, supporting more accurate, reproducible, and methodologically grounded work.

items.title: Co-designing VR chemistry labs: Pre–post learning changes, reshaped classroom dynamics & deployment lessons for real-world rollout in post-primary schools
items.abstract: Experiential learning is central to chemistry education, yet post-primary schools face persistent constraints related to cost, safety, and infrastructure that limit hands-on laboratory access. While immersive VR has demonstrated potential for conceptual and procedural learning, comparatively less is known about how VR-based procedural chemistry learning can be co-designed for adolescents, integrated with teacher orchestration, and implemented under authentic school constraints. This paper investigates how Virtual Reality (VR) can be designed and implemented as a deployable, pedagogically grounded classroom infrastructure for post-primary chemistry education. We report findings from a 25-month, three-phase participatory co-design study involving 137 stakeholders, including students, teachers, pre-service teachers, school leaders, parents, and domain experts. The study culminated in the development and real-world classroom deployment of a VR-based acid–base titration experience. Quantitative analyses showed significant pre–post increases following participation in the VR experience in conceptual knowledge (pre: M = 7.81, post: M = 9.52, p < .001) and curriculum-aligned procedural knowledge (pre: M = 4.71, post: M = 9.14, p < .001). Qualitative findings indicated learner autonomy, confidence, and engagement during VR-supported activities. Beyond individual learning outcomes, the study illustrates how VR can reshape classroom ecology by enabling self-paced procedural practice and shifting teacher roles toward facilitation and orchestration. Findings also highlight the need to balance adolescent learners’ autonomy with appropriate scaffolding through adjustable guidance, pacing control, and on-demand support. Finally, the study identifies key sociotechnical conditions for sustainable classroom integration, including alignment with teacher practices, assessment needs, and classroom constraints. By linking learning outcomes with classroom deployment and design rationale, this work contributes a holistic account of how immersive technologies can move beyond novelty toward viable use in post-primary education.

items.title: Co-Modifying Application Code and Deployment Infrastructure: A Causal Study of AI Agent Pull Requests
items.abstract: Current software engineering agents are evaluated predominantly inside isolated sandboxes against synchronous local tests. However, deploying features in collaborative repositories requires modifying continuous integration (CI/CD) pipelines, containers, and provisioning manifests alongside application logic. Because agents lack deployment awareness, attempting cross-domain modifications introduces unverified dependencies into asynchronous integration pipelines. To isolate the causal integration overhead of dual-scope pull requests (PRs)-modifying both application code and deployment infrastructure-we evaluated 26,999 PRs across two large datasets (AIDev v5 and MOSAIC-3M) encompassing six agent architectures and an aligned human baseline. Using a deterministic four-tier file taxonomy and an exact 4D strata-matching framework, we isolated integration metrics under conditional exchangeability while controlling for application volume. We find agents operate primarily as application coders or chore workers, with maintenance tasks capturing 17.70% to 25.41% of agent PRs. Dual-scope modifications represent only 4.48% to 4.55% of agentic PRs, yet trigger bimodal integration outcomes. In the first mode, explicitly reviewed contributions experience protracted delays, adding a median penalty of +13.13 hours and multiplying time-to-merge by 3.24x, driven mechanically by CI/CD and provisioning manifests. In the second mode, maintainer gatekeeping exhibits a structural bypass: even for external contributors lacking repository write access, agent identity reduces the odds of human review by 63.7% compared to human peers. Consequently, 43.1% to 56.2% of dual-scope PRs bypass inspection to merge silently in a median of under 31 minutes. These uninspected modifications compromise build verification, demonstrating the need for deployment-aware benchmarks and strict path-based access controls.

items.title: Coarse-to-Fine Label Distribution Learning for High-Cardinality Survey Simulation
items.abstract: Modeling fine-grained survey distributions for high-cardinality large language model prediction is challenging under mixed-cardinality supervision. Because low-cardinality surveys dominate training, standard label distribution learning (LDL) develops positional bias toward early response regions and fails to generalize probability allocation to extended spaces. This bias collapses probability mass into low-index regions, thereby fragmenting high-cardinality distributions. To address this, the authors propose hierarchical LDL, a coarse-to-fine framework using macroscopic anchors to calibrate fine-grained predictions. By jointly optimizing hierarchical distributions, hierarchical LDL stabilizes probability allocation across sparsely supervised high-cardinality scales and improves structural alignment.

items.title: COFFEQA: Counterfactual-Guided Few-Shot Distillation for LLM Question Answering
items.abstract: Knowledge distillation aims to train a smaller student model to mimic a larger teacher model for resource-constrained environments. However, the process of distillation is typically data-intensive and computationally expensive, particularly for generative tasks. Few-shot distillation offers an alternative by transferring teacher knowledge using limited training samples. However, we observe that few-shot distillation performance is heavily dependent on the choice of these training samples. In fact, we demonstrate that using more uncertain samples near the teacher's decision boundary can significantly deteriorate distillation performance. Motivated by this observation, we propose Counterfactual-guided Few-shot Distillation in Open-book Question Answering (COFFEQA), a novel strategy that aptly uses counterfactuals to provide additional supervision around challenging factual samples. In the generative QA setting, we define a counterfactual as a minimally modified context that induces the teacher to change its response to an alternative answer. We provide geometric insights on how factual-counterfactual pairs can constrain the deviation between the teacher's and student's decision boundaries. We further introduce a new metric, Context Following Difficulty (CFD) that further validates counterfactuals prior to distillation based on agreement with the intended alternative answer and dependence on the modified context. COFFEQA uses CFD-validated factual-counterfactual pairs for few-shot distillation. Experiments across five in-domain and three out-of-domain QA benchmarks using T5 and Qwen2.5 families show that COFFEQA outperforms factual-only distillation baselines under the same few-shot budget. For instance, on TriviaQA, COFFEQA improves over the factual-only baseline by 8.77 average EM points and 9.98 average F1 points under the T5 setting with 32 few-shot pairs.

items.title: Cognitive Ergonomics in Robotics
items.abstract: Work tasks performed by humans within any work system are the connecting elements between humans and other system elements such as deployed technologies. Fundamental to any task performance are mental processes of those individuals acting within any socio-technical system. Perception, attention, learning, memory and reasoning are just examples of these processes. Within human factors, they are typically studied to evaluate, for instance, mental workload and situation awareness of technology users, whose errors can dramatically impact the safety and the performance of the system. Accordingly, this chapter presents concepts from cognitive ergonomics. These concepts should be considered within Human–Robot Interaction (HRI) studies and applications in order to assess and improve the design of robots which can interact with humans in terms of technology acceptance, usability, accessibility, and, overall, user experience. This chapter describes different effects on humans related to the interaction with robotic systems. Furthermore, specific HRI design elements and recommendations will be outlined. The chapter closes with an overview on quantitative and qualitative methods proposed to evaluate and to assess different aspects of HRI.

items.title: Collaborative Learning and Reasoning over Model Slices
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel across diverse tasks, benefiting from knowledge priors, in-context reasoning, and test-time computation. Despite these strengths, single-model reasoning remains vulnerable to error propagation, as later steps depend on the model's earlier outputs, leaving reasoning blind spots difficult to independently reassess. To address this limitation, we develop \textit{collaborative learning}, encompassing the construction of heterogeneous collaborators and the learning of effective cross-model collaboration. Specifically, \textit{model slicing} replaces a large model with smaller, heterogeneous models under a comparable parameter budget, enabling prior reasoning to be reassessed across distinct model parameterizations. \textit{Pyramid supervision} combines protocol distillation with step-level supervision to refine reasoning and interaction decisions throughout collaboration. We evaluate our approach across four task categories: multi-hop question answering, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and open-ended constrained generation. The trained heterogeneous models achieve comparable or better task performance than the original large model and established multi-agent baselines, including reinforcement-learning-based methods, while also achieving higher inference efficiency than the multi-agent baselines and exhibiting differentiated collaboration patterns across tasks. These findings show that learned collaboration turns model heterogeneity into complementary reasoning capabilities.

items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong individual task performance, yet still struggle to collaborate with users over extended, multi-turn interactions, for example by attempting solutions before understanding the user's needs or by failing to revise mistaken assumptions after receiving feedback. We propose Collaborative Theory of Mind (CToM), a framework that addresses these challenges by explicitly training LLMs to anticipate user responses and to use those predictions to improve their own behavior. CToM drafts a response, predicts how the user will respond, and uses this prediction to guide internal revision before presenting a response. During training, the user's reply to each draft serves as the target for predicting the next turn, and we train the assistant to minimize the negative log-likelihood of that reply. We combine this prediction objective with group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) to optimize both task performance and interaction efficiency. Across mathematical reasoning, coding, and writing tasks, CToM achieves higher collaborative task performance than all baselines; for example, on a collaborative mathematical reasoning task, it improves final accuracy from 74.1% to 79.6% compared with naive GRPO. Ablations show that predicting user responses also makes collaboration more efficient: under the same reward, adding prediction supervision reduces the number of user replies by 8% on coding and 17% on writing while improving task performance. Behavioral analyses of interaction trajectories show that user-response predictions become more accurate after training, and that more accurate predictions are associated with larger improvements in collaborative task performance through self-revision.

items.title: Colleagues that work together move together: How co-moving among newcomers affects individual and team performance.
items.abstract: As teams and team membership become more dynamic, colleagues from the same prior team increasingly transition together to a new team as a cohort: a phenomenon known as co-moving. Drawing on theories of shared team experience and team receptivity, we develop a multilevel, multi-theory, and multi-period model to examine how co-moving affects individual and team performance. We theorize that co-movers carry forward proximal shared team experience which they can leverage immediately to support their own performance relative to solo movers, who must build new working relationships. However, we also theorize that co-movers’ proximal shared team experience hinders team performance, though these detrimental effects attenuate over time. We test our theory using archival data from the National Basketball Association, supplemented by qualitative interviews with individuals involved in professional basketball. Our findings reveal that co-movers exhibit better individual performance than solo movers on their new teams and in our robustness checks we find that greater shared tenure on the prior team further enhances this advantage. At the team level, teams with co-movers perform worse than teams with solo movers, and we find partial support that this disadvantage attenuates over time. Additional analyses show that co-movers’ individual performance advantage persists over time in the new team. The findings from our interviews illuminate how these processes unfold both on and off the court. Our research contributes to the literature on shared team experience and newcomer integration by highlighting a multilevel tradeoff: while co-moving benefits individuals, it can initially undermine collective performance.

items.title: Community pharmacists’ acceptance and willingness to adopt artificial intelligence for medication counseling: a cross-sectional study in Jordan
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly being incorporated into healthcare delivery. This study aimed to assess pharmacists' perceptions, acceptance, and readiness to adopt Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies to support medication counseling in community pharmacy practice. A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 300 community pharmacists in Jordan between February and March 2026. Acceptance of AI was assessed using the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM). The survey collected data on perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, behavioral intention, prior AI experience, perceived benefits, and concerns regarding AI use. Logistic regression analysis was performed to identify factors associated with willingness to adopt AI in medication counseling. This study included a total of 300 community pharmacists. Overall, pharmacists demonstrated positive perceptions of AI technologies. Most participants were familiar with AI tools (n = 283, 94.3%) and reported using them in daily life (n = 222, 74.0%), although most had not received formal AI training (n = 185, 61.7%). More than half were willing to integrate AI into medication counseling (n = 156, 52.0%), while 104 (34.7%) were uncertain and 40 (13.3%) were unwilling. The most commonly perceived benefits were improved patient education (n = 204, 68.0%), drug interaction checking (n = 200, 66.7%), and counseling efficiency (n = 197, 65.7%). Major concerns included inadequate regulation (n = 218, 72.7%), AI accuracy (n = 205, 68.3%), and data privacy (n = 205, 68.3%). Our model demonstrates that behavioral intent is the primary source of willingness to adopt AI (AOR = 1.966, 95% CI: 1.212–3.188; p = 0.006), while younger age was also associated with greater willingness (AOR = 0.947, 95% CI: 0.915–0.980; p = 0.002). Community pharmacists generally viewed AI as a valuable adjunct to medication counseling rather than a replacement for professional judgment. Addressing concerns related to regulation, training, data privacy, and AI reliability will be essential for the successful integration of AI into pharmacy practice.

items.title: Comparative evaluation of three large language models for fixed prosthodontic treatment planning: a standardized scenario-based study
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being explored for clinical and educational applications in dentistry. However, their ability to generate comprehensive fixed prosthodontic treatment plans has not been adequately compared under standardized conditions. This study aimed to compare the quality of prosthodontic treatment plans generated by Qwen 3.7 Plus (Qwen), Claude Sonnet 5 (Claude), and Mistral Medium 3.5 (Mistral). Thirty standardized prosthodontic clinical scenarios were presented to each LLM, yielding 90 treatment plans. Two blinded prosthodontic evaluators independently assessed each plan with a seven-domain, five-point Likert-scale rubric covering diagnostic accuracy, treatment selection, treatment sequencing, completeness, reference adherence, patient safety, and overall clinical appropriateness. Evaluator scores were averaged for the primary analysis. Differences among models were assessed with the Friedman test, followed by paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm adjustment. Inter-rater agreement was assessed with quadratic-weighted Cohen’s κ and a two-way mixed-effects ICC (single- and average-measure). A sensitivity analysis evaluated whether model rankings remained consistent when each evaluator was analyzed separately. In the primary analysis of averaged evaluator scores, Qwen had the highest mean total score (33.82 ± 1.74), followed by Claude (32.52 ± 2.30) and Mistral (29.68 ± 2.66) (Friedman χ² (2) = 35.05, p < 0.001; Kendall’s W = 0.584). All three pairwise comparisons were significant after Holm adjustment. Across individual domains, Qwen scored highest for completeness and reference adherence, while Claude achieved the highest patient safety scores. However, inter-rater agreement was poor, with a single-measure ICC of 0.378 and an average-measure ICC of 0.549. Sensitivity analysis revealed that the model ranking was not consistent across evaluators: Evaluator 1 ranked Claude marginally higher than Qwen, whereas Evaluator 2 ranked Qwen clearly higher than Claude. This discrepancy was associated with a pronounced ceiling effect in Evaluator 1’s ratings, who assigned the maximum score to the majority of Qwen and Claude cases. Qwen achieved the highest mean score in the primary analysis, with particular strengths in completeness and reference adherence, while Claude showed the highest patient safety scores. However, the model ranking was not consistent across evaluators, and Mistral had the lowest mean score across all seven domains. Ceiling effects and limited inter-rater agreement were observed, and these findings do not support universal superiority of any single model. From a dental education perspective, LLMs may have potential as adjunctive tools for case-based learning and critical appraisal of treatment-planning decisions, but educational effectiveness was not directly assessed in this study.

items.title: Comparative Study of IC Engine and Electric Powertrains for Go-Kart Applications
items.abstract: A go-kart is a small, lightweight four-wheeled vehicle designed for recreational, educational and competitive driving. This project deals with the design and fabrication of a go-kart powered by an internal combustion (IC) engine. The main objective is to develop a simple, strong, economical and serviceable vehicle using commonly available mechanical components and workshop processes. The project covers the selection of the IC engine, chassis design, steering system, braking system, power transmission, wheels and tyres, accelerator and control mechanism. The frame is designed to support the engine, driver and other components while maintaining adequate rigidity and stability. The engine converts the chemical energy of fuel into mechanical power, which is transmitted to the driving axle through a suitable transmission arrangement. The methodology includes requirement identification, conceptual design, component selection, basic engineering calculations, CAD/drawing preparation, material procurement, fabrication, assembly and testing. The report also discusses important safety aspects such as braking performance, steering response, chain guarding, fastener tightening and driver protection. The project provides practical understanding of automobile engineering, IC engines, manufacturing processes, machine design, welding, power transmission and vehicle testing. The final design can be further improved by reducing weight, improving ergonomics, optimizing power transmission and introducing additional safety and instrumentation.

items.title: Conceptual Overlap Between OPTIMAL Theory Constructs and Motor Presentations in Functional Neurological Disorder Rehabilitation
items.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Functional neurological disorder (FND) is increasingly recognized as a disorder of brain network dysfunction with neuroimaging studies demonstrating altered communication among neural circuits involved in movement, attention, and self-agency. The Optimizing Performance Through Intrinsic Motivation and Attention for Learning (OPTIMAL) theory of motor learning is centered on the three constructs: external focus of attention, enhanced expectancies, and autonomy. This article explores the potential alignment between the pathophysiology underlying FND and the constructs proposed by the OPTIMAL theory and hypothesizes that OPTIMAL offers a promising, pathophysiology-informed framework for the physical therapy management of FND across varied practice settings. SUMMARY OF KEY POINTS: • FND is characterized by disrupted brain network communication, particularly in circuits related to motor learning, attention, and self-agency.• Physical therapy is supported by evidence as a first-line treatment for motor symptoms in FND; however, existing consensus guidelines do not identify an explicit motor learning framework to guide PT intervention• The OPTIMAL theory of motor learning emphasizes external focus of attention, enhanced expectancies, and autonomy, constructs that align with the neural networks implicated in FND and have demonstrated efficacy to improve motor learning when applied to healthy and neurological populations. RECOMMENDATIONS FOR CLINICAL PRACTICE: • Applying motor learning constructs from OPTIMAL offers a practical and evidence-aligned approach to treating motor learning deficits in FND across care settings and age groups.• Therapists may improve motor outcomes in FND by incorporating external cueing, success-oriented feedback, and patient choice.

items.title: Conclusion: Synthesis and a research agenda for nature-based tourism
items.abstract: Purpose This paper concludes the special issue “Reimagining Nature-Based Tourism: Innovations, Experiences and Sustainability in Tourism Destinations” by synthesising the 11 contributions through a thematic synthesis approach and outlining an agenda for future research. Design/methodology/approach The paper adopts a thematic synthesis approach. The eleven articles included in this special issue were coded against the issue's guiding research question and three derived sub-questions, and grouped into six cross-cutting themes. The contributions span qualitative interview-based case studies, analysis of visitor-generated online content and bibliometric analysis. Findings The synthesis shows that nature-based tourism destinations convert natural resources into sustainable visitor value only when aesthetic appeal is matched by interpretive depth and infrastructural investment; that human intermediaries, community enterprises and certification bodies jointly, and sometimes unevenly, mediate conservation outcomes; and that digital methods and artificial intelligence are reshaping both how sustainability discourse is understood and how destinations might be managed, while introducing new risks of standardisation and dehumanisation. Originality/value This original concluding article brings together eleven geographically and methodologically diverse studies through a structured, research-question-driven synthesis, translating individual contributions into a shared reference framework and research agenda for nature-based tourism scholarship and destination practice.

items.title: Consequential Behaviour and Representational Fairness in the Validation of Synthetic Research
items.abstract: Researchers in industry and academia use synthetic survey respondents powered by large language models as substitutes for human samples. These synthetic populations require validation against real-world data, so researchers often address them using ad hoc comparisons with human surveys. Inspired by the intention–behaviour gap in behavioural science, we argue that these validations test the wrong thing for most applied cases where decision makers commission synthetic research to anticipate consequential behaviour. To address this problem, we propose a validation framework with two requirements. First, every validity claim must state its level of correspondence with human data: does the sample predict what the represented people do, which of four diagnostics (location, dispersion, response process and structure) does the validation address, and does the validation compare against experimental effects? Second, researchers must report validity claims for subgroups, since these groups are often the most affected by consequential decisions and aggregate accuracy hides their misrepresentation. Our validation framework operationalises three justice dimensions (distributional, procedural, and recognition) as measurable quantities and treats within-persona counterfactual experiments as a design that itself requires validation. We then apply the framework to electric vehicle charging tariffs, before closing with a reporting checklist that researchers can use to make convincing validity claims.

items.abstract: Contextual vectors are the working objects of contemporary language models: a token, once placed in a window, is assigned a vector that depends on that window. A growing literature then reads geometry in the resulting space as evidence of intelligence, of a consciousness spectrum, or of situational awareness. This article reinterprets that move with the criterion isolated in the companion teaching note. A multidimensional array is not a tensor. It becomes the component representation of a geometric object only when a transformation law is stated and an invariant is named. Applied here, the criterion separates three things that the consciousness literature collapses. The first is a representation map from contexts to a fibre. The second is a self-locating competence, measured behaviorally by out-of-context reasoning and by the Situational Awareness Dataset. The third is an identity claim, associated with integrated information theory, on which experience is a cause-effect structure. Only the first is mathematics of the vector. The second is a family of tasks. The third is a metaphysical identification that no embedding entails. 1. The conflation KS The reinterpretation is constructive. Context is treated as a base, the contextual vector as a coordinate representation of a section, and situational content as an invariant functional of that section, stable under the redescriptions the theory itself allows. items.title: Contractual and Liability Issues in AI Educational Technologies
items.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into educational technologies has significantly transformed teaching, learning, and administrative processes within modern educational systems. AI-driven tools such as intelligent tutoring systems, automated grading platforms, and predictive learning analytics offer opportunities for personalized learning, improved efficiency, and enhanced academic outcomes. However, the increasing reliance on these technologies also raises important contractual, regulatory, and liability concerns, particularly within the evolving legal framework of the Indian education sector. This study examines the contractual governance and liability allocation associated with AI educational technologies by analyzing stakeholder perceptions of contractual clarity, regulatory compliance, ethical safeguards, and institutional support mechanisms. Using an empirical mixed-methods research design, data were collected from 300 stakeholders including AI developers, educational administrators, teachers, and students across four South Indian states.

items.title: Convergence Between Artificial Intelligence and Digital Purchasing Behavior
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming digital behavior and consumer decision-making, reshaping interactions between individuals and brands across digital platforms. This chapter analyzes the relationship between digital behavior, AI, and marketing strategies in a changing technological context. It examines how AI-driven tools, such as predictive analytics and automated recommendation systems, enable content personalization, improve user experiences, and increase marketing effectiveness. Based on contemporary literature and secondary data from sources including Statista, Pew Research Center, Pordata and Euromonitor, the study adopts an exploratory approach to assess AI's impact on consumer engagement and strategic marketing practices. It also discusses ethical challenges, such as data privacy, algorithmic bias, and manipulation risks. The research offers insights for scholars and practitioners on AI's growing influence and highlights the need for future qualitative studies on consumer perceptions.

items.title: Creativity in design education: an educational psychology model of motivation, cognitive load, and self-efficacy
items.abstract: Objective This study examines the statistical relationships among learning motivation, cognitive load, creative self-efficacy, and expert-rated creative performance among undergraduate design students. Methods A quantitative cross-sectional study was conducted with 428 valid responses from undergraduate students majoring in design-related disciplines. Students first completed a design task, after which questionnaire data were collected and anonymized design works were evaluated by three independent experts. SPSS was used for descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, correlation analysis, regression-based path analysis, and Bootstrap tests of statistical indirect effects; AMOS was used to evaluate the measurement model. Results Learning motivation and germane cognitive load were positively associated with creative self-efficacy. Creative self-efficacy showed the strongest positive association with design creative performance, and germane cognitive load showed a smaller positive direct association. Extraneous cognitive load was negatively correlated with creative performance at the bivariate level, but its adjusted direct path was not statistically significant; therefore, H5 was not supported. Intrinsic cognitive load was not significant. Bootstrap results indicated significant statistical indirect relationships through creative self-efficacy. Conclusion The findings suggest that design creativity is associated with students' motivation, meaningful cognitive engagement, and creative self-beliefs. Because the questionnaire was administered after the design task, the indirect effects should be interpreted as statistical indirect relationships rather than evidence of causal or temporal mediation.

items.title: CRISIS RESOURCE MANAGEMENT (CRM) COURSE FOR UNDERGRADUATE MEDICINE AND NURSING STUDENTS
items.abstract: Background Crisis Resource Management (CRM) is a key framework for optimizing team dynamics, communication, situational awareness, and non-technical skills in high-pressure healthcare environments. Although well established in postgraduate medical education, its implementation in undergraduate curricula remains limited. This study aims to describe the educational design, implementation, and outcomes of a simulation-based CRM program for final-year medical and nursing students. Activity Development (Methods) Conducted annually since the 2018–2019 academic year at Universidad Francisco de Vitoria, the mandatory program is structured around 15 core CRM principles across five domains: role clarity, communication, seeking/managing help, resource utilization, and global assessment. Sessions are facilitated by trained instructors and simulation technicians. The educational format includes pre-course materials, an introductory psychological safety and video analysis session, equipment familiarization stations, and four high-fidelity simulation scenarios (cardiac arrest, hypoglycemia with altered consciousness, acute pulmonary edema, and major trauma). Interprofessional teams (two medical and three nursing students) participate actively in scenarios followed by structured plus/delta/plus debriefings. Perceptions and satisfaction are gathered via post-activity surveys. Discussion & Practical Implications The interprofessional approach is identified as one of the program’s most valuable aspects, fostering collaborative problem-solving, shared leadership, and mutual role understanding prior to independent clinical practice. Participants report high satisfaction and express strong support for increased interprofessional training. Study limitations include the absence of a control group, reliance on self-reported perception data, and lack of long-term objective evaluation in real-world clinical settings. Conclusions High-fidelity simulation-based CRM training provides an effective, highly accepted educational framework for undergraduate medical and nursing students, promoting teamwork competencies and fostering a patient safety culture early in clinical training.

items.title: Current Diagnostic Approaches to Pulpal and Periapical Diseases
items.abstract: The success of endodontic treatment largely depends on establishing an accurate diagnosis and selecting an appropriate treatment strategy based on the available diagnostic findings. Pulpal and periapical diseases may present with overlapping clinical and radiographic features, while certain non-endodontic conditions can also mimic endodontic disease. These similarities may complicate diagnosis, particularly when symptoms are nonspecific, pulpal tests provide inconclusive results, or radiographic findings are limited. Therefore, endodontic diagnosis should be based on the integration of the patient’s history, clinical examination, pulpal and periapical tests, and radiographic findings. When necessary, advanced diagnostic methods, including cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) and histopathological examination, can provide additional information. An accurate differential diagnosis is essential not only for identifying the underlying condition but also for avoiding unnecessary endodontic or surgical procedures and establishing an appropriate treatment plan. When the expected healing does not occur after treatment or the clinical course is inconsistent with the initial diagnosis, the diagnosis should be reconsidered. In recent years, the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in endodontics has introduced new opportunities to support diagnostic assessment. AI-based applications have increasingly been investigated for tasks such as radiographic image analysis, detection of periapical lesions, assessment of root canal morphology, determination of working length, and identification of vertical root fractures. However, AI should not be regarded as an independent diagnostic method that replaces clinical assessment. Rather, it should be considered a supportive tool that may facilitate a more systematic and objective interpretation of clinical and radiographic data . Integrating clinical expertise with contemporary technological advances may improve diagnostic accuracy and contribute to more appropriate treatment planning in endodontics.

items.title: Curriculum Design and Evaluation of Data Science Track for Management Students
items.abstract: The growing demand for data science competencies across professional fields creates a need for curricula that enable management students to develop analytical skills while navigating increasingly complex technological environments. This study examines the design and evaluation of a three-year Data Science track embedded within an undergraduate management program. The curriculum integrates statistics, programming, data management, visualization, artificial intelligence, and project-based learning within a progressively structured, multi-tool environment. A multi-cohort, multi-method design combined longitudinal academic performance data from two independent cohorts with graduates’ attitudes toward data science, career adaptability, course perceptions, and qualitative feedback. Academic performance showed cohort-specific patterns: variability decreased progressively across the three years in Cohort 1, whereas in Cohort 2 it decreased in the second year but increased in the third year. Graduates reported high perceived utility and interest in data science, relatively high career adaptability, and positive perceptions of applied and project-oriented courses, although self-efficacy varied in technically demanding areas. Qualitative findings highlighted authentic projects, progressive learning, and multi-tool exposure, alongside challenges related to technical complexity. The study provides program-level evidence for designing accessible yet rigorous data science curricula and highlights the potential value of progressive curricular integration and applied multi-tool learning for management students.

items.title: Cybersecurity Behavior in AI Vibe Coding: Extending Technology Threat Avoidance Theory
items.abstract: Generative AI has rapidly reshaped software development, fueling “vibe coding,” in which developers increasingly rely on AI-generated code. While offering productivity benefits, this practice raises important cybersecurity concerns. Drawing on Technology Threat Avoidance Theory (TTAT), this study examines developers’ cybersecurity behavior in AI-assisted coding environments. Survey data from 358 participants with recent AI coding-assistant experience were analyzed using PLS-SEM. Security self-efficacy exhibited the largest positive effect on cybersecurity behavior, followed by perceived threat, while trust in AI had a smaller positive effect. AI transparency and perceived risk showed no significant direct effects. Perceived severity and susceptibility positively shaped perceived threat, supporting TTAT’s core threat-appraisal mechanism. The model explained 44.5% of the variance in cybersecurity behavior. PLSpredict provided evidence of out-of-sample predictive performance. The findings clarify TTAT’s applicability and theoretical boundaries in AI-mediated software development and offer practical implications for developers, organizations, and AI tool providers seeking safer AI-assisted coding practices.

items.title: Data governance, business strategy, and sustainability practices: exploratory employee-perception evidence from a single pulp and paper corporate group
items.abstract: Purpose This study examines how data governance (DG) contributes to environmental, social, and governance (ESG) integration by strengthening data accountability, the reliability of ESG-related information, and strategic alignment. Grounded in the resource-based view (RBV), it investigates the relationships among DG, Business Strategy (BS), and sustainability practices and principles (SPP) within a single pulp and paper organisation. Design/methodology/approach This study adopts a bounded single-organisation employee survey design based on non-probabilistic convenience sampling. Survey data were collected from 103 valid respondents within one pulp and paper corporate group and analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling to examine perceived associations among DG, BS, and SPP. The analysis was complemented by contextual information on the organisation's DG model and its integration with operational excellence to support ESG objectives. Findings Within the studied organisation, the results suggest positive direct and indirect associations among DG, BS, and SPP. The indirect association through BS is statistically significant and consistent with partial mediation, suggesting that BS may play an alignment role between DG and SPP. The findings provide exploratory, context-specific evidence that respondents perceive DG as associated with the organisational embedding of ESG principles when aligned with BS, particularly through the reliability, traceability, and strategic use of ESG-related information. Research limitations/implications The study is limited by its focus on a single industry and cross-sectional design, which may affect generalisability. Future research should explore longitudinal approaches and extend the model to other sectors. Additionally, the role of emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence in strengthening DG and ESG integration warrants further investigation. Practical implications Organisations should treat DG as a strategic capability rather than a compliance function. Integrating DG into BS and OPEX frameworks may strengthen perceived data quality, transparency, and decision-making. Establishing clear governance structures, roles, and data standards may support perceived ESG alignment and sustainability-oriented organisational practices. Social implications By promoting transparency, accountability, and ethical data use, DG may strengthen the organisational conditions associated with ESG-related decision-making and stakeholder trust. The study does not directly measure external social outcomes, environmental performance, or stakeholder perceptions. Originality/value This study advances existing DG and sustainability research by examining DG, BS, and SPP as interrelated constructs within a single RBV-informed empirical model. It shows how governed data capabilities may support ESG integration both directly and through strategic alignment.

items.title: Data Science for the Next Millennium: A Ubiquitous Review
items.abstract: Data science has grown from a set of statistical and computational techniques into a field that brings together different disciplines to turn complex data into useful insights. This review looks at how data science was defined, applied, and studied across different fields from 2018 to 2023. The review followed a structured approach and drew on research identified through several scholarly sources. The initial search found 105 articles in databases and platforms including EBSCO, Taylor & Francis, Wiley, Sage, Emerald, and Google Scholar. After screening, 40 studies were examined in detail. The review considered each study’s purpose, findings, application area, country, analytical tools, and research type. The findings show that data science brings together computer science, statistics, business analysis, engineering, machine learning, automation, and subject-specific knowledge. Education and healthcare were the most common areas of application in the studies reviewed. Researchers used a wide range of methods and tools, including machine learning, artificial intelligence, regression, neural networks, data mining, SQL, Python, R, CRISP-DM, statistical analysis, optimization, and data visualization. Empirical research made up the largest share of the studies, though conceptual papers and reviews also contributed to the field. Overall, the review suggests that successful data science depends on more than algorithms. It also requires reliable data, privacy safeguards, relevant skills, thoughtful interpretation, ethical practice, and a clear understanding of the problem being addressed.

items.abstract: Artificial intelligence increasingly informs consequential enterprise decisions, yet prevailing governance approaches tend to assess ethical principles, model properties, regulatory conformity or audit activities in isolation. This conceptual paper argues that trustworthy AI governance should focus on the organizational decision supported by AI rather than on the model alone. It develops Decision Assurance by Design, a capability framework that embeds assurance requirements across the AI lifecycle and connects trustworthy AI principles to organizational capabilities, operational controls, assurance evidence and explicit decision authorization. items.title: DecoAR: An Intelligent Mobile Augmented Reality and Generative AI Framework for Spatial Interior Design
items.abstract: The prevailing consumer workflow for furniture selection and interior space planning still depends on manual dimension estimates and static visual judgment, which places a heavy cognitive burden on shoppers and contributes to elevated post-purchase return rates. This paper presents DecoAR, a native Android application that unifies markerless Augmented Reality (AR) with multi-modal Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) to give users an in-situ, dimensionally accurate way to plan interior spaces. DecoAR is implemented with a declarative Jetpack Compose interface and is built on Google’s ARCore tracking subsystem, wrapped by the SceneView library and its Filament-based Physically Based Rendering (PBR) pipeline. The system contributes four coordinated capabilities: (i) markerless placement and gesture-based manipulation of 3D furniture assets on detected planes, (ii) a point-to-point spatial tape measure derived from 3D Euclidean geometry, (iii) real-time, flicker-free vertical-plane repainting for wall color testing, and (iv) an AI design assistant that reads the live Filament frame buffer and forwards it to Google’s Gemini 2.5 Flash model for context-aware layout feedback. Layouts are persisted locally through a reactive, GSON-serialized repository backed by shared preferences, so that users can save, reload, and share designs without a dedicated database engine. Empirical trials show sustained rendering at 60 frames per second (FPS) under standard furniture-placement workloads, a floor of 52 FPS under combined wall-painting and background AI transfer, and sub-2.1cm spatial measurement error even on low-texture surfaces. Unlike prior AR furniture visualizers, which function largely as passive object renderers, and prior generative-design tools, which reason over static images or floor-plan text rather than a live tracked scene, DecoAR couples geometry-grounded AR state directly to a vision-language model in a single closed loop. The results indicate that consumer-grade mobile hardware is now capable of hosting real-time spatial reasoning and generative design feedback within a single, responsive application.

items.title: Decoding Consumer Engagement Mechanisms in LLM-Enabled Environments
items.abstract: This study examined the mechanisms that shape consumer engagement in Large Language Model enabled environments by integrating statistical and data driven analytical approaches. Primary data were collected from users with experience in interacting with LLM driven systems. Exploratory Factor Analysis identified the core dimensions underlying engagement related perceptions, while Multiple Regression Analysis examined the influence of technological, psychological, and experiential factors on consumer engagement. Machine learning techniques including classification, clustering, principal component analysis, and feature ranking were employed to enhance predictive accuracy and interpretability. The findings revealed that user motivation, perceived social presence, and trust in the system emerged as dominant drivers of engagement. The study contributes to a deeper understanding of consumer engagement dynamics in intelligent conversational environments and offers practical insights for effective LLM based interaction design.

items.title: Decoupling multi-source interference and time-varying parameters in laser echo signals for non-cooperative target detection
items.abstract: Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) has become a pivotal technology for non-cooperative target detection and characterization in space situational awareness, on-orbit servicing, and deep-space exploration, owing to its high spatial resolution and precise ranging capability. Nevertheless, complex dynamic space environments introduce coupled temperature-vibration interference and time-varying distance/incidence angle parameters, triggering severe nonlinear fluctuations in laser echo intensity. Conventional LiDAR reconstruction methods based on the ideal Lambertian surface assumption fail to decouple such nonlinear modulation effects, resulting in prominent deviations in material property inversion. To address this issue, this paper proposes an instantaneous state sampling and parametric decoupling method for laser echo signals from non-Lambertian surfaces. Specifically, a Wendland C 2 -Gaussian hybrid interpolation model is established to characterize the temperature-vibration coupling effect, and a momentum-enhanced stochastic Bregman proximal gradient (MSBPG) algorithm is developed for global optimization. Combined with the Cook-Torrance bidirectional reflectance distribution function for target surface modeling, the proposed method effectively decouples temperature-vibration coupling disturbances from time-varying spatial modulation factors. Validated on a semi-physical simulation platform with controllable temperature field and multi-axis vibration excitation, the proposed method achieves superior performance under typical compound interference conditions (353 K thermal radiation and 25 Hz mechanical vibration). Quantitative results demonstrate that the MSBPG algorithm reduces the training-set decoupling root mean square error (RMSE) by 34.2% compared with the conventional Bregman proximal gradient method, with a low test-set RMSE of 0.026. Moreover, the proposed approach decreases the RMSE of emissivity estimation by 65.6% relative to the traditional Lambertian-based correction method. This work provides a high-precision, physically interpretable technical solution for robust non-cooperative target recognition and dynamic material characterization in harsh space environments.

items.title: Delegating decision authority to AI in recruitment: an empirical study of trust, control and algorithmic accountability
items.abstract: Purpose The widespread adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in human resource (HR) practices has led to a growing number of organizations trying to understand the use of AI in recruitment. While AI is increasingly embedded in HR practices, few studies focus on how trust in AI is formed and how it shapes the adoption of AI in recruitment. Design/methodology/approach This study employed a qualitative research design based on 21 semi-structured interviews with HR professionals working in large, internationally operating German family-owned organizations that use AI in recruitment. The data was analysed using a theory-guided qualitative approach following the Gioia methodology to construct a systematic data structure linking participants’ experiences to established theoretical dimensions of trust. Findings The findings reveal that trust in AI is shaped by three interrelated dimensions: ability, integrity and benevolence. The study underscores how trust serves as a dynamic slider that governs the degree of decision authority delegated to AI systems, varying from automated screening for habitual tasks to human oversight for complex, cognitive tasks. Key tensions also emerge around power, control and trust breakdown. Practical implications First, the study emphasizes that organizations should recognize that successful AI adoption depends not only on technical performance, but also on deliberate trust-building strategies. By investing in transparency mechanisms, such as explainable AI interfaces, organizations can get a clear understanding of how recruitment algorithms operate. Second, organizations should invest in structured training programs to develop the efficiency and confidence of HR professionals working with AI systems. This can be done by offering training that focusses on interpreting algorithmic outputs, recognizing potential biases and maintaining ethical oversight. Third, organizations should establish formal governance frameworks that define accountability, certification standards and internal usage guidelines, which can reduce uncertainty and promote consistent, responsible AI practices in recruitment practices. Originality/value The study contributes to the technology acceptance model (TAM) and the algorithmic accountability theory by demonstrating how trust conditions the adoption of AI in recruitment. It theorizes how micro-level trust judgements are structurally conditioned by macro-level institutional safeguards and provides empirical insights into how HR professionals balance human judgement and algorithmic decision-making.

items.title: Demographic Differences in Automated Facial Attractiveness Prediction: Evidence from SCUT-FBP5500 and MEBeauty
items.abstract: In this work, we examine automated facial beauty prediction (FBP) models to evaluate demographic variation in human attractiveness scores, facial landmark preprocessing, and cross-dataset prediction error. We perform multistage quantitative sociotechnical audits using SCUT-FBP5500 and a 1,962-image MEBeauty subset, including DLib landmark-extraction analysis, intersectional ordinary least squares (OLS) regression, observed-rating inter-rater variability analysis, and a five-seed ResNet-50 cross-dataset evaluation. DLib landmark extraction was successful for 1,929 of 1,962 MEBeauty images, with an overall failure rate of 1.7%. The highest observed subgroup failure rate was among Middle Eastern men (4.2%; 2/48). In the symmetry-adjusted OLS model (N = 1,929, R² = .022), no gender, ethnicity, or gender × ethnicity coefficient was statistically significant at the Benjamini–Hochberg correction. At the same time, blur was the sole significant image quality control (p=.006). Subgroup RMSE estimates across datasets ranged from .470 to .512. Black men had the highest point estimate (RMSE = .512), but prespecified image-level bootstrap comparisons with Asian men (difference = .002, 95% CI [−.09, .09]) and White men (difference = .022, 95% CI [−.05, .09]) both included zero. These results show how disaggregated sociotechnical auditing can be useful and also emphasize the significance of disentangling descriptive subgroup variation from statistically supported demographic disparities.

items.abstract: A go-kart is a small, lightweight four-wheeled vehicle designed for recreational, educational and competitive driving. This project deals with the design and fabrication of a go-kart powered by an internal combustion (IC) engine. The main objective is to develop a simple, strong, economical and serviceable vehicle using commonly available mechanical components and workshop processes. The project covers the selection of the IC engine, chassis design, steering system, braking system, power transmission, wheels and tyres, accelerator and control mechanism. The frame is designed to support the engine, driver and other components while maintaining adequate rigidity and stability. The engine converts the chemical energy of fuel into mechanical power, which is transmitted to the driving axle through a suitable transmission arrangement. The methodology includes requirement identification, conceptual design, component selection, basic engineering calculations, CAD/drawing preparation, material procurement, fabrication, assembly and testing. The report also discusses important safety aspects such as braking performance, steering response, chain guarding, fastener tightening and driver protection. The project provides practical understanding of automobile engineering, IC engines, manufacturing processes, machine design, welding, power transmission and vehicle testing. The final design can be further improved by reducing weight, improving ergonomics, optimizing power transmission and introducing additional safety and instrumentation.
